definition: Text Nailing (TN) is an information extraction method used in the fields of natural language processing (NLP), computational linguistics, and health informatics.
details: It was developed to address challenges in extracting structured, analyzable data from large volumes of unstructured text such as clinical notes, research articles, and other narrative documents. Unlike fully automated machine learning systems, Text Nailing emphasizes a "human-in-the-loop" approach: a person interactively reviews small portions of text to identify expressions that are common, non-negated, and semantically informative. These "nailed expressions" are then converted into simplified alphabetical-only forms, creating consistent and homogeneous representations of the text. This hybrid strategy allows TN to combine the precision of expert-guided annotation with the scalability of computational techniques. The method has been applied to improve predictive modeling in medicine, enhance the performance of text classifiers, and reduce reliance on large manually labeled datasets.

tiers.eli5: A person scans small bits of a long document and marks the phrases worth keeping, which a computer then turns into tidy rows of data.
tiers.practitioner: Unlike fully automated machine learning systems, it uses a human-in-the-loop approach where a person reviews small portions of text to identify expressions that are common, non-negated, and semantically informative. The pitfall is that the human review step does not scale as freely as fully automated pipelines.
tiers.paperLevel: An information extraction method in which a person interactively reviews small portions of text to identify common, non-negated, semantically informative "nailed expressions", which are then converted into simplified structured data; it emphasizes a human-in-the-loop approach rather than full automation.

explainer.example: A reviewer marks common, non-negated phrases in a sample of clinical notes, and those expressions become structured fields in a database.
